transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just cannot keep my mind on one single thing anymore. It's getting really bad. Like, I'll be in the shop, and just one saw starting up, or somebody walking past the office window, or even just me having a thought about another job, and I'm completely pulled off what I’m doing. 

Which, actually, we're doing this big custom cabinetry job over on Elm Street right now, and the client wants this very specific reclaimed oak. It's gorgeous wood, really, but the supplier is just... I mean, you wouldn't believe the shipping delays right now. My brother-in-law drives a freight truck, and he was telling me the other day about how backed up the distribution yards are, and he says it's mostly because of the... wait. I'm sorry, what was I saying? 

Oh, right. Yeah, so I just get sidetracked by every little thing, and then I look at the clock and the whole day has just completely gotten away from me.
Looking back at your time in grade school, did you experience these same struggles with staying focused and getting easily distracted back then?

Oh, yeah. Definitely. Even way back then, like, long before I was 12. My teachers were always pulling my mother aside to tell her I was a bright girl, but just... careless. I was always losing my homework, or I'd completely forget the instructions the second the teacher finished talking. I spent half my childhood staring out the classroom window instead of finishing my seatwork. 

I remember in fourth grade, my desk was right next to this big window that looked out over the playground and this massive old elm tree. We had so many elm trees in my neighborhood growing up, you know, before the Dutch elm disease wiped most of them out. My dad actually had to cut ours down himself in the front yard. He had this old McCulloch chainsaw, loud as anything, and it smoked like crazy. He used to let me help him stack the firewood, which is probably where I got my start working with wood, honestly. He built us this incredible treehouse out of the scraps, and my brother and I would... um. 

I'm sorry, I did it again, didn't I? What did you ask me about my teachers?
Aside from the trouble with focus, would you say you often feel restless, like you have a motor running inside you, or do you frequently find yourself interrupting others when they are speaking?

Well, no, not really interrupting people, I don't think. But the restless part... yeah, actually. If I have to sit at the desk doing estimates for jobs, or if I have to sit through a long meeting with a contractor, I get so wound up inside. It's like I just need to get up and move around. 

Which has been really hard lately because I hurt my wrist a while back. I was helping a buddy frame out a shed and I just lost my footing. It's healed up now, mostly, but the doctor told me I need to take it easy on the heavy lifting for a bit. Which is fine, I know I'm supposed to just stay put and finish the paperwork side of things, but it's just... I hate paperwork. I've always hated it. My ex-husband used to do all the books for the business before we split, and he was a real stickler for keeping every single receipt. He had this whole filing system with color-coded tabs, and he'd spend hours every Sunday just... wait. 

Sorry. What were we talking about? The estimates?

When you are in those situations where you feel that internal restlessness, do you find that you also feel a strong, uncontrollable urge to fidget, tap your feet, or move around while you are trying to stay seated?

No, not really. I don't sit there tapping my feet or squirming around like that. It's just that tight, wound-up feeling inside. Plus, honestly, it's hard to tap your feet when you're wearing heavy steel-toe boots all day anyway. 

I've been wearing the exact same brand of boots for... gosh, twenty years now. Thorogoods. They take an absolute age to break in, let me tell you. I remember when I bought my very first pair, I wore them straight to this big framing job out in the county, building a wraparound porch for this lovely older couple. The husband used to come out every single day at noon with iced tea for the crew. Real sweet guy. He used to be a mechanic for Ford before he retired, and he had this pristine 1968 Mustang in the garage. Cherry red. He was telling me all about how hard it is to find original parts for the carburetor these days, because everything is just manufactured so cheap now, and... um. 

Wait. I'm doing it again. What did you ask me about my boots?
Do you find that you often talk excessively, even when you aren't trying to tell a story or explain your work?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I definitely talk a lot, you can probably tell that by now, but it's usually just me trying to explain something or tell a story. I don't just sit there chattering away for no reason. 

Like, if I'm on a job site, I have to talk a lot to explain to the younger guys how to cut the joints right. You wouldn't believe how many kids come out of trade school these days and don't know how to do a proper dovetail joint. They all just want to use a nail gun and call it a day. I had this one kid, maybe twenty-two, working for me last summer. Sweet kid, but completely useless with a hand saw. He was always talking about his podcasts. He listened to these true crime podcasts all day long while he worked, which I always thought was a bit morbid, honestly. I prefer listening to the classic rock station, myself. Bob Seger, Tom Petty... you know, music you can actually work to. I saw Tom Petty live back in '89, I think it was. It rained the whole time, but nobody cared. We were all just out there in the mud, singing along to 'Free Fallin' and... 

Oh, gosh. I'm sorry. Did you ask me about my crew?
